hook: A seismograph, a heart monitor and a motion detector all draw a wave-like trace across a screen. When the trace comes from a mass on a spring, you can read everything about the motion from it: how far the mass swings, how long each swing takes, and where it moves fastest.

figure.caption: Position, velocity and acceleration over one period, lined up in time.

chain.cause: A restoring force F = −kx acts on the object
chain.effect: its acceleration is always opposite to its displacement, so the a-t graph is the x-t graph flipped

chain.cause: The object turns around at x = ±A
chain.effect: its velocity is zero there: the x-t graph is flat at its peaks and troughs

chain.cause: The object passes x = 0 with no force to slow it yet
chain.effect: its speed is greatest there: the x-t graph is steepest where it crosses zero

chain.cause: Doubling the amplitude doubles the force and the speed at each matching point
chain.effect: the cycle takes the same time: the period does not depend on the amplitude

ideas: Position in SHM is x = A cos(2πft) if the object starts at +A, or x = A sin(2πft) if it starts at equilibrium moving in +x. Use radians.
On an x-t graph: the height of a peak is A; the time from peak to peak is T; the slope is the velocity.
Speed is greatest at x = 0 and zero at x = ±A. Acceleration is zero at x = 0 and largest at x = ±A, always pointing toward equilibrium.
The period does not depend on the amplitude: a bigger swing has more distance to cover and covers it faster.

misconception.wrong: The object moves fastest at the turning points, because that is where the force on it is largest.
misconception.right: A large force means a large acceleration, not a large speed. At the turning points the object is momentarily at rest; it is fastest at equilibrium, where the force is zero.

summary: SHM is described by x = A cos(2πft) or A sin(2πft); on the graphs, speed is greatest and acceleration zero at equilibrium, speed zero and acceleration greatest at the turning points, and the period is independent of the amplitude.
